summary: Lists the requirements that congestion control mechanisms should meet for interactive, point-to-point real-time media such as video calls. Such traffic needs low delay and tolerates some loss, so it differs from bulk transfers and web browsing. The requirements are meant for judging candidate algorithms, particularly for WebRTC-style RTP traffic. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When many cars share a road, they must not all rush in at once or everybody gets stuck. This document lists the good manners that video-call traffic should follow so it shares the road fairly without making calls choppy.

subtitle: Eleven requirements a congestion control algorithm should meet for live, interactive media such as video calls.

tldr.problem: TCP congestion control was built for bulk transfers and web pages. Interactive real-time media needs data delivered continuously within hundreds of milliseconds, can tolerate some loss, and is often rate limited by the application.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists eleven requirements for a congestion control algorithm for interactive point-to-point real-time media, covering delay, fairness, startup, stability, feedback and queue behaviour. It also explains why TFRC does not meet them.
tldr.outcome: The requirements serve as a yardstick for judging candidate algorithms, mainly for RTP traffic such as WebRTC. The document is informational and sets no protocol.

facts.label: Delay budget
facts.value: No more than hundreds of milliseconds end to end

facts.label: Quick reaction
facts.value: A few RTTs, likely within a second

today: RFC 8836 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is meant as a set of requirements for judging congestion control for interactive real-time media, and it pairs with RFC 8868, which covers evaluating such algorithms.

sections.title: Why Real-Time Media Is Different
sections.content:
Most TCP congestion control schemes were developed for reliable bulk transfer of non-time-critical data, such as large files. They have also been used for fetching web pages and for non-interactive streaming video, where the data must be ready when the viewer wants it but exact timing does not matter.

Interactive real-time media is different. Data must flow continuously within a very limited time window, with no more delay than hundreds of milliseconds end to end. The sources can often adapt how much they send, but they may be rate limited by the application and may not always have data to send. Some packet loss is tolerable, but data delivered late is commonly useless, and sending "future" data is impossible.

Other kinds of flows will still be present, so the algorithm must work properly with them as cross traffic.

The focus is WebRTC, where two peers send multiple RTP flows plus data flows at the same time, without special arrangements with the service providers in between. RTP has no congestion control of its own, so circuit breakers such as those in RFC 8083 are required to protect the network from non-congestion-controlled flows.

When the media is congestion controlled, the mechanism is recommended to operate within the constraints of those circuit breakers when one is present, and should not cause congestion collapse when none is implemented. Non-interactive media such as video streaming, and multicast or broadcast technologies, are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A video call is like a live conversation, so late words are useless. The rules are for calls between two people, not movies or broadcasts.

sections.title: Delay, Fairness and Startup Requirements
sections.content:
Requirement 1 says the algorithm MUST attempt to provide as-low-as-possible-delay transit while still providing a useful amount of bandwidth. It should minimize self-induced latency even with intermediate bottlenecks and competing flows, and should react quickly to events such as routing changes or interface changes (for example WLAN to 3G data). A quick reaction means on the order of a few RTTs, likely within a second; reacting on the very next RTT is explicitly not required, since many codecs cannot adapt that quickly.

Requirement 2 says the algorithm MUST be fair to other flows, both real-time flows such as other instances of itself and TCP flows. Existing flows must also let new flows ramp up to a useful share. Requirement 3 says it SHOULD NOT starve competing TCP flows, and when low delay and a useful bandwidth share conflict, the useful share takes priority.

Requirement 4 says the algorithm SHOULD adapt as quickly as possible to the initial network conditions, whether the starting bandwidth is above or below the bottleneck. Starting too low can ruin the "Hello!" moment of a call, while starting too high causes other problems, so there is a tension.
sections.plainLanguage: The call should keep delay small, share fairly with downloads, and figure out the right speed quickly when it starts, without shoving others aside.

sections.title: Stability, Multiple Streams and Queues
sections.content:
Requirement 5 says the algorithm SHOULD be stable when RTP streams halt or are discontinuous, for example with Voice Activity Detection, and should regain its previous share rapidly after a pause. Requirement 6 says that where possible it SHOULD merge information across RTP streams between two endpoints that share a bottleneck, and share information with non-RTP flows such as a WebRTC data channel. When several streams share a 5-tuple, the application should be able to control how bandwidth is split.

Requirement 10 says it SHOULD treat an unexpected lack of backchannel information as a possible sign of channel overuse. Requirement 11 says it SHOULD stay stable and keep delay low when faced with Active Queue Management (AQM).

The algorithm must also avoid building queues when competing with short bursts, such as web browsing, and must not add to delay buildup during bursts from periodic flows such as MPEG DASH.
sections.plainLanguage: If the call goes quiet, it should pick up politely where it left off. It should also notice when messages from the other side stop arriving, because that may mean trouble.

sections.title: Feedback and Network Signals
sections.content:
Requirement 7 says the algorithm SHOULD NOT require special support from network elements. It should use information already available about the incoming flow: packet arrival times, acknowledgements and feedback, packet timestamps, packet losses and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN).

Requirement 8 says the backchannel typically SHOULD be the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP), using a profile such as RTP/AVPF (RFC 4585) or RTP/SAVPF (RFC 5124) that allows frequent enough feedback. Feedback should be kept small, for example with the reduced-size techniques of RFC 5506, and can be sent less often when conditions are stable.

Requirement 9 says the algorithm SHOULD try to use DSCP markings when they are available, since a bottleneck may or may not honor them.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver sends short progress notes back to the sender. They should be quick enough to help but small enough not to clog the way back.

sections.title: Why TFRC Falls Short
sections.content:
TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC, RFC 5348) is the existing mechanism that claims to suit real-time interactive media. It is equation-based, fair to TCP and has lower throughput variation, at the price of a slower response to bandwidth changes. The RFC names several deficiencies.

  • It only treats loss events as a congestion signal, even though large network buffers add delay.
  • It is designed for a smooth rate, but media sources change rate in steps and video encoders can vary output bitrate a lot.
  • It works in bytes per second or packets per second, while media sources work in bits per second.
  • It increases by at most twice the current rate, which causes problems when video bitrates vary.

A variant, TFRC-SP (RFC 4828), helps small-packet audio but TFRC remains less optimal for video. The RFC concludes that the requirements cannot be met by TFRC as defined in the standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The older fair-sharing method was made for steady traffic, but a video call speeds up and slows down in jumps, so it does not fit well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who can delete, delay or insert messages can fake congestion signals unless they travel on a tamper-proof path. Because some algorithms depend on packet arrival timing, even a protected channel does not fully mitigate this.

Attacks that reduce bandwidth are not necessarily significant, since an on-path attacker could break the connection by discarding all packets. Attacks that increase the perceived available bandwidth need evaluation, as they could starve competing flows and permit amplification attacks. Designers should consider malicious on-path attackers.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone sitting in the middle could send false signals that the road is empty, and that could make the call crowd out others.
